Single-Loop Stochastic Projected Damped Extragradient Methods for Stochastic Nonconvex–(Strongly) Concave Minimax Optimization

Huiling Zhang ††thanks: The first two authors contributed equally to this paper. Affiliation: LSEC, ICMSEC, Academy of Mathematics and Systems Science,Chinese Academy of Sciences, Beijing 100190, China Email: zhanghl@amss.ac.cn    Minhao Zhang11footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, College of Sciences, Shanghai University,Shanghai 200444, Chinazhangminhao@shu.edu.cn; xuzi@shu.edu.cn    Zi Xu ††thanks: Corresponding author. Affiliation: Department of Mathematics, College of Sciences, Shanghai University,Shanghai 200444, Chinazhangminhao@shu.edu.cn; xuzi@shu.edu.cn
Abstract

We develop single-loop stochastic projected damped extragradient methods for stochastic nonconvex–(strongly) concave minimax optimization, with complexity guarantees for both game stationarity (GS) and optimization stationarity (OS). Our approach combines a stochastic projected damped extragradient (SPDE) method with a recursive variance-reduced variant, VR-SPDE, both of which retain a single-loop structure. Under an unbiased stochastic gradient oracle with uniformly bounded variance, SPDE finds an ε\varepsilon-game-stationary point with stochastic first-order oracle (SFO) complexities of O⁡(κ​ε−4)O(\kappa\varepsilon^{-4}) and O⁡(ε−5)O(\varepsilon^{-5}) in the nonconvex–strongly concave and nonconvex–concave settings, respectively, where κ=L/μ\kappa=L/\mu. Under an additional mean-square Lipschitz condition on the stochastic gradients, VR-SPDE improves these GS complexities to O⁡(κ3/2​ε−3)O(\kappa^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3}) and O(ε−9/2)O(\varepsilon^{-9/2}), respectively. For an ε\varepsilon-optimization-stationary point, SPDE achieves SFO complexities of O⁡(κ​ε−4)O(\kappa\varepsilon^{-4}) and O⁡(ε−6)O(\varepsilon^{-6}), while VR-SPDE achieves O⁡(κ3/2​ε−3)O(\kappa^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3}) and O⁡(ε−6)O(\varepsilon^{-6}), in the two settings, respectively. These OS guarantees match the best-known bounds achieved by multi-loop methods while preserving a single-loop implementation. To the best of our knowledge, our results provide the best-known SFO complexity guarantees among single-loop stochastic first-order methods for the respective stationarity criteria and problem classes.

Keywords: stochastic nonconvex–(strongly) concave minimax optimization; stochastic projected damped extragradient method; variance reduction; single-loop algorithms.

1 Introduction

We consider the stochastic minimax problem

minx∈X⁡maxy∈Y⁡F⁡(x,y):=𝔼ω∼𝒟​[f⁡(x,y,ω)],\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}F(x,y):=\mathbb{E}_{\omega\sim\mathcal{D}}[f(x,y;\omega)], (1)

where X⊆ℝnX\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} is closed and convex, Y⊆ℝpY\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p} is compact and convex, and FF is smooth. The objective may be nonconvex in xx and is concave or strongly concave in yy. The random variable ω\omega follows an unknown distribution 𝒟\mathcal{D}, and 𝔼\mathbb{E} denotes expectation. Problems of this form arise in distributed nonconvex optimization [4], wireless systems [1], and statistical learning [12]. Their growing scope of applications motivates stochastic first-order methods that combine a simple iteration structure with strong oracle complexity guarantees.

Two stationarity criteria are central to nonconvex minimax optimization: game stationarity (GS) and optimization stationarity (OS). Game stationarity concerns first-order conditions for the two players at a primal–dual pair, whereas optimization stationarity concerns the minimization of the primal value function

ϕ⁡(x):=maxy∈Y⁡F⁡(x,y).\phi(x):=\max_{y\in Y}F(x,y).

These criteria capture different aspects of approximate solutions, and their complexity guarantees must be distinguished. This distinction is particularly relevant in the nonconvex–concave setting, where ϕ\phi may be nonsmooth. We state the precise GS and OS criteria in Section 2 and analyze both criteria for the methods developed in this paper.

For stochastic nonconvex–strongly concave problems, representative multi-loop methods obtain strong stochastic first-order oracle (SFO) complexity guarantees by approximately solving an inner maximization problem or a regularized saddle-point subproblem. Luo et al. [8] proposed SREDA, which combines nested ascent with SPIDER recursion and requires O⁡(κ3​ε−3)O(\kappa^{3}\varepsilon^{-3}) stochastic gradient evaluations, where κ=L/μ\kappa=L/\mu, LL is the gradient Lipschitz constant, and μ\mu is the strong concavity parameter. Zhang et al. [15] developed SAPD+, which combines an inexact proximal-point outer scheme with an accelerated primal–dual inner solver. Their method requires O⁡(L​κ​ε−4)O(L\kappa\varepsilon^{-4}) oracle calls, while its variance-reduced variant requires O⁡(L​κ2​ε−3)O(L\kappa^{2}\varepsilon^{-3}) calls. Among single-loop methods, Lin et al. [7] analyzed two-timescale stochastic gradient descent–ascent (SGDA) and established an O⁡(κ3​ε−4)O(\kappa^{3}\varepsilon^{-4}) stochastic gradient complexity for value-function stationarity. Huang et al. [5] introduced Acc-MDA with a STORM-type estimator and obtained complexities of O~​(κ9/2​ε−3)\widetilde{O}(\kappa^{9/2}\varepsilon^{-3}) without a large batch and O~​(κ5/2​ε−3)\widetilde{O}(\kappa^{5/2}\varepsilon^{-3}) with a batch size of order κ4\kappa^{4}.

For stochastic nonconvex–concave problems, the possible nonsmoothness of the value function presents an additional challenge. Multi-loop methods often address this difficulty through proximal regularization or regularized saddle-point subproblems. Zhang et al. [15] applied SAPD+ to this setting and established an O⁡(ε−6)O(\varepsilon^{-6}) oracle complexity. Among single-loop methods, Lin et al. [7] established an O⁡(ε−8)O(\varepsilon^{-8}) stochastic gradient complexity for SGDA under value-function stationarity. For game stationarity, Zhang and Xu [14] proposed FORMDA, which combines vanishing dual regularization with recursive momentum and achieves an iteration complexity of O~(ε−13/2)\widetilde{O}(\varepsilon^{-13/2}).

These results highlight the challenge of obtaining strong complexity guarantees within a single-loop implementation. Multi-loop methods achieve sharper dependence on the target accuracy in several settings, but their outer iterations may require inner maximization, proximal, or regularized saddle-point subproblems to be solved to prescribed accuracies. The resulting inner-loop lengths and parameter schedules can depend on the target accuracy. This motivates the following question:

Can single-loop stochastic first-order methods achieve improved game-stationarity guarantees and match the best-known multi-loop optimization-stationarity guarantees for both nonconvex–strongly concave and nonconvex–concave problems?

We address this question through a stochastic projected damped extragradient method and its recursive variance-reduced variant. Both methods retain a single-loop structure, and their analysis provides complexity guarantees for both GS and OS.

Contributions.

Our contributions concern the algorithmic design and the complexity guarantees under the two stationarity criteria.

  1. (i)

    Single-loop stochastic damped extragradient methods. We propose a stochastic projected damped extragradient (SPDE) method under an unbiased stochastic gradient oracle with uniformly bounded variance. We further incorporate a recursive variance-reduction mechanism to obtain VR-SPDE under an additional mean-square Lipschitz condition on the stochastic gradients. Both algorithms use a single-loop structure without nested iterative solvers for maximization, proximal, or saddle-point subproblems.

  2. (ii)

    Complexity guarantees for game stationarity. SPDE finds an ε\varepsilon-game-stationary point with total SFO complexities of O⁡(κ​ε−4)O(\kappa\varepsilon^{-4}) and O⁡(ε−5)O(\varepsilon^{-5}) in the nonconvex–strongly concave and nonconvex–concave settings, respectively. The corresponding iteration complexities are O⁡(κ​ε−2)O(\sqrt{\kappa}\varepsilon^{-2}) and O(ε−5/2)O(\varepsilon^{-5/2}). Under the additional mean-square Lipschitz condition, VR-SPDE improves the GS oracle complexities to O⁡(κ3/2​ε−3)O(\kappa^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3}) and O(ε−9/2)O(\varepsilon^{-9/2}), respectively, while preserving the single-loop structure.

  3. (iii)

    Complexity guarantees for optimization stationarity. For an ε\varepsilon-optimization-stationary point, SPDE requires O⁡(κ​ε−4)O(\kappa\varepsilon^{-4}) and O⁡(ε−6)O(\varepsilon^{-6}) SFO calls in the nonconvex–strongly concave and nonconvex–concave settings, respectively. VR-SPDE achieves the corresponding complexities of O⁡(κ3/2​ε−3)O(\kappa^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3}) and O⁡(ε−6)O(\varepsilon^{-6}). These OS guarantees match the best-known multi-loop dependence on the target accuracy in both settings while retaining a single-loop implementation.

To the best of our knowledge, these results provide the best-known total SFO complexity guarantees among single-loop stochastic first-order methods for the respective stationarity criteria and problem classes. In particular, the same single-loop algorithms support both GS and OS guarantees. In the strongly concave setting, the two criteria have the same stated SFO bounds for each method. In the merely concave setting, the GS bounds are O⁡(ε−5)O(\varepsilon^{-5}) for SPDE and O(ε−9/2)O(\varepsilon^{-9/2}) for VR-SPDE, whereas both methods attain an OS bound of O⁡(ε−6)O(\varepsilon^{-6}). Table 1 summarizes representative results and identifies the stationarity criterion associated with each bound.

In Table 1, NC–SC and NC–C denote the nonconvex–strongly concave and nonconvex–concave settings, respectively. “VR” indicates whether a method uses recursive variance reduction, and “GS” and “OS” denote game stationarity and optimization stationarity. The Acc-MDA entry reports the bound without a large batch. Each result is stated under the assumptions of the corresponding reference; comparisons must account for both the stationarity criterion and the stochastic oracle assumptions.

Organization and notation.

Section 2 presents the preliminaries and defines the GS and OS criteria. Section 3 introduces SPDE and its stochastic oracle model, develops a unified convergence analysis, and establishes the GS complexity bounds for the nonconvex–strongly concave and nonconvex–concave settings. Section 4 introduces the paired oracle, recursive estimator, and VR-SPDE algorithm, and derives the corresponding variance-reduced GS complexity bounds with all oracle calls counted. Section 5 establishes the OS guarantees for the original primal value function. Section 6 concludes the paper.

Throughout, ∥⋅∥\lVert\cdot\rVert denotes the Euclidean norm, ⟨⋅,⋅⟩\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle denotes the corresponding inner product, and ΠC\Pi_{C} and NCN_{C} denote the Euclidean projection onto and the normal cone of a closed convex set CC, respectively. The notation O⁡(⋅)O(\cdot) suppresses constants independent of the target accuracy ε\varepsilon and of any parameters whose dependence is displayed explicitly. The notation O~​(⋅)\widetilde{O}(\cdot) additionally suppresses logarithmic factors.

2 Preliminaries and stationarity criteria

We first state the standing assumptions and then introduce the stationarity criteria used in our complexity analysis. Throughout, product spaces are equipped with the Euclidean norm.

Assumption 1.
  1. (i)

    The set X⊆ℝnX\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{n} is nonempty, closed, and convex. The set Y⊆ℝpY\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{p} is nonempty, compact, and convex, with

    DY:=maxy∈Y⁡∥y∥>0.D_{Y}:=\max_{y\in Y}\lVert y\rVert>0.
  2. (ii)

    For almost every ω\omega, the sample loss f⁡(⋅,⋅,ω)f(\cdot,\cdot;\omega) is differentiable on a neighborhood of X×YX\times Y.

  3. (iii)

    The function FF is continuously differentiable on a neighborhood of X×YX\times Y, and there exists L>0L>0 such that, for all (x,y),(x′,y′)∈X×Y(x,y),(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})\in X\times Y,

    ∥∇F​(x′,y′)−∇F​(x,y)∥≤L⁡∥(x′−x,y′−y)∥.\lVert\nabla F(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})-\nabla F(x,y)\rVert\leq L\lVert(x^{\prime}-x,y^{\prime}-y)\rVert. (2)
  4. (iv)

    For every x∈Xx\in X, the function F⁡(x,⋅)F(x,\cdot) is concave on YY. The primal value function satisfies

    ϕ⁡(x):=maxy∈Y⁡F⁡(x,y),x∈X,ϕinf:=infx∈Xϕ⁡(x)>−∞.\phi(x):=\max_{y\in Y}F(x,y),\qquad x\in X,\qquad\phi_{\inf}:=\inf_{x\in X}\phi(x)>-\infty. (3)

Compactness of YY and continuity of FF ensure that the maximum in (3) is attained for every x∈Xx\in X. The quantity DYD_{Y} bounds the norm of points in YY; it is not the diameter of YY.

In the nonconvex–strongly concave setting, we additionally assume that F⁡(x,⋅)F(x,\cdot) is μ\mu-strongly concave on YY, uniformly in x∈Xx\in X, for some μ>0\mu>0. Equivalently, for every x∈Xx\in X and y,y′∈Yy,y^{\prime}\in Y,

F⁡(x,y′)≤F⁡(x,y)+⟨∇yF​(x,y),y′−y⟩−μ2​∥y′−y∥2.F(x,y^{\prime})\leq F(x,y)+\langle\nabla_{y}F(x,y),y^{\prime}-y\rangle-\frac{\mu}{2}\lVert y^{\prime}-y\rVert^{2}.

We write κ:=L/μ\kappa:=L/\mu in this setting. The stochastic oracle assumptions are stated separately with the corresponding algorithms.

Projection and normal cone.

For a nonempty closed convex set C⊆ℝdC\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}, define

ΠC(w):=argminu∈C12∥u−w∥2,NC(u):={{η∈ℝd:⟨η,a−u⟩≤0​for all ​a∈C},u∈C,∅,u∉C.\Pi_{C}(w):=\argmin_{u\in C}\frac{1}{2}\lVert u-w\rVert^{2},\qquad N_{C}(u):=\begin{cases}\{\eta\in\mathbb{R}^{d}:\langle\eta,a-u\rangle\leq 0\ \text{for all }a\in C\},&u\in C,\\ \varnothing,&u\notin C.\end{cases} (4)

The projection is uniquely defined and satisfies

u=ΠC(w)⟺w−u∈NC(u),∥ΠC(w)−ΠC(w′)∥≤∥w−w′∥.u=\Pi_{C}(w)\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad w-u\in N_{C}(u),\qquad\lVert\Pi_{C}(w)-\Pi_{C}(w^{\prime})\rVert\leq\lVert w-w^{\prime}\rVert. (5)

For a nonempty set AA, we use dist⁡(v,A):=infa∈A∥v−a∥\dist(v,A):=\inf_{a\in A}\lVert v-a\rVert.

Game stationarity.

For a feasible pair (x,y)∈X×Y(x,y)\in X\times Y, define the game-stationarity residual of the original minimax problem by

ℛ​(x,y)2:=dist2⁡(0,∇xF​(x,y)+NX​(x))+dist2⁡(0,−∇yF​(x,y)+NY​(y)).\mathcal{R}(x,y)^{2}:=\dist^{2}\bigl(0,\nabla_{x}F(x,y)+N_{X}(x)\bigr)+\dist^{2}\bigl(0,-\nabla_{y}F(x,y)+N_{Y}(y)\bigr). (6)

Thus ℛ⁡(x,y)=0\mathcal{R}(x,y)=0 if and only if

0∈∇xF​(x,y)+NX​(x),0∈−∇yF​(x,y)+NY​(y).0\in\nabla_{x}F(x,y)+N_{X}(x),\qquad 0\in-\nabla_{y}F(x,y)+N_{Y}(y).

These inclusions express the first-order conditions for the minimization and maximization variables, respectively. By concavity of F⁡(x,⋅)F(x,\cdot), the second inclusion is equivalent to y∈arg⁡maxv∈Y⁡F⁡(x,v)y\in\arg\max_{v\in Y}F(x,v).

We call a random feasible pair (xout,yout)(x_{\rm out},y_{\rm out}) ε\varepsilon-game-stationary in expectation if

𝔼⁡[ℛ​(xout,yout)2]≤ε2.\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathcal{R}(x_{\rm out},y_{\rm out})^{2}\bigr]\leq\varepsilon^{2}. (7)

By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, this condition also implies

𝔼⁡[ℛ⁡(xout,yout)]≤ε.\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathcal{R}(x_{\rm out},y_{\rm out})\bigr]\leq\varepsilon.
Optimization stationarity.

Optimization stationarity concerns the constrained minimization of the primal value function ϕ\phi. To incorporate the constraint explicitly, define

ϕ¯​(x):={ϕ⁡(x),x∈X,+∞,x∉X.\bar{\phi}(x):=\begin{cases}\phi(x),&x\in X,\\ +\infty,&x\notin X.\end{cases}

For each y∈Yy\in Y, Assumption 1 implies that F⁡(⋅,y)F(\cdot,y) is LL-weakly convex on XX; that is,

x⟼F⁡(x,y)+L2​∥x∥2x\longmapsto F(x,y)+\frac{L}{2}\lVert x\rVert^{2}

is convex on XX. Taking the pointwise maximum over y∈Yy\in Y shows that ϕ\phi is also LL-weakly convex on XX. Moreover, continuity of FF and compactness of YY imply that ϕ\phi is continuous relative to XX. Consequently, ϕ¯\bar{\phi} is a proper, lower semicontinuous, LL-weakly convex function on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}.

For z∈ℝnz\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, define the Moreau envelope of ϕ¯\bar{\phi} with parameter 1/(2​L)1/(2L) and its associated proximal point by

p0​(z):=minx∈X⁡{ϕ⁡(x)+L​∥x−z∥2},x0⋆​(z):=argminx∈X{ϕ⁡(x)+L​∥x−z∥2}.p_{0}(z):=\min_{x\in X}\left\{\phi(x)+L\lVert x-z\rVert^{2}\right\},\qquad x_{0}^{\star}(z):=\argmin_{x\in X}\left\{\phi(x)+L\lVert x-z\rVert^{2}\right\}. (8)

Since 1/(2​L)<1/L1/(2L)<1/L, the standard Moreau-envelope theorem for weakly convex functions guarantees that x0⋆​(z)x_{0}^{\star}(z) exists and is unique for every z∈ℝnz\in\mathbb{R}^{n}. Furthermore, p0p_{0} is continuously differentiable on ℝn\mathbb{R}^{n}, with

∇p0​(z)=2​L​(z−x0⋆​(z)).\nabla p_{0}(z)=2L\bigl(z-x_{0}^{\star}(z)\bigr). (9)

We therefore use the optimization-stationarity measure

𝒮OS​(z):=∥∇p0​(z)∥.\mathcal{S}_{\rm OS}(z):=\lVert\nabla p_{0}(z)\rVert. (10)

A random output zout∈ℝnz_{\rm out}\in\mathbb{R}^{n} is called ε\varepsilon-optimization-stationary in expectation if

𝔼⁡[𝒮OS​(zout)2]≤ε2.\mathbb{E}\bigl[\mathcal{S}_{\rm OS}(z_{\rm out})^{2}\bigr]\leq\varepsilon^{2}.

This condition also implies 𝔼⁡[𝒮OS​(zout)]≤ε\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{S}_{\rm OS}(z_{\rm out})]\leq\varepsilon.

The GS criterion measures first-order residuals at a feasible primal–dual pair, whereas the OS criterion measures the gradient of a Moreau envelope of the constrained primal value function. The envelope is defined for every z∈ℝnz\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, and its proximal point x0⋆​(z)x_{0}^{\star}(z) always belongs to XX. Although the two criteria are related, their approximate guarantees are not interchangeable without further analysis. We establish the corresponding complexity bounds separately.

3 A stochastic projected damped extragradient method

We develop a stochastic projected damped extragradient (SPDE) method for nonconvex–(strongly) concave minimax optimization. The method combines a projected predictor–corrector step, a damped dual momentum recursion, and a relaxed update of a primal proximal center. These updates are performed within a single loop: each iteration uses a fixed sequence of projections and stochastic gradient queries, without an inner iterative solver for a regularized saddle-point subproblem. In this section, we establish the game-stationarity guarantees; the corresponding optimization-stationarity guarantees are developed in Section 5.

Regularized objective.

For a center z∈Xz\in X and a regularization parameter 0<τ≤L0<\tau\leq L, define

g⁡(x,y,z,ω)\displaystyle g(x,y;z,\omega) :=f⁡(x,y,ω)+L​∥x−z∥2−τ2​∥y∥2,\displaystyle:=f(x,y;\omega)+L\lVert x-z\rVert^{2}-\frac{\tau}{2}\lVert y\rVert^{2}, (11)
G⁡(x,y,z)\displaystyle G(x,y;z) :=𝔼ω∼𝒟​[g⁡(x,y,z,ω)]=F⁡(x,y)+L​∥x−z∥2−τ2​∥y∥2.\displaystyle:=\mathbb{E}_{\omega\sim\mathcal{D}}[g(x,y;z,\omega)]=F(x,y)+L\lVert x-z\rVert^{2}-\frac{\tau}{2}\lVert y\rVert^{2}.

Under Assumption 1, F⁡(⋅,y)F(\cdot,y) is LL-weakly convex on XX. Consequently, for each fixed zz, G⁡(⋅,⋅,z)G(\cdot,\cdot;z) is LL-strongly convex in xx and τ\tau-strongly concave in yy. If F⁡(x,⋅)F(x,\cdot) is μ\mu-strongly concave, the dual strong concavity modulus of GG is μ+τ\mu+\tau. These properties concern the population objective GG; they need not hold for individual sample objectives gg. The regularized objective guides the algorithmic updates. The stationarity criteria remain those of the original problem: the residual ℛ\mathcal{R} in (6) and the Moreau-envelope measure 𝒮OS\mathcal{S}_{\rm OS} in (10). The effect of dual regularization on these criteria is accounted for in the subsequent complexity analysis.

Stochastic gradient estimates.

For a feasible query point u=(x,y)u=(x,y) and a batch Ω=(ω1,…,ωm)\Omega=(\omega_{1},\ldots,\omega_{m}) of independent samples from 𝒟\mathcal{D}, define

∇^​F​(u,Ω):=1m​∑i=1m∇f​(x,y,ωi).\widehat{\nabla}F(u;\Omega):=\frac{1}{m}\sum_{i=1}^{m}\nabla f(x,y;\omega_{i}). (12)

The regularization gradients are evaluated exactly, so stochastic estimation is needed only for ∇F\nabla F.

At iteration tt, SPDE queries three fresh batches sequentially: at the current iterate, at a projected predictor, and at the corrected iterate. We use the notation

g^t(0)\displaystyle\widehat{g}_{t}^{(0)} :=∇^​F​((xt,yt),Ωt(0)),\displaystyle:=\widehat{\nabla}F((x_{t},y_{t});\Omega_{t}^{(0)}), (13)
g^t(1)\displaystyle\widehat{g}_{t}^{(1)} :=∇^​F​((x~t,y~t),Ωt(1)),\displaystyle:=\widehat{\nabla}F((\widetilde{x}_{t},\widetilde{y}_{t});\Omega_{t}^{(1)}),
g^t(2)\displaystyle\widehat{g}_{t}^{(2)} :=∇^​F​((xt+1,yt+1),Ωt(2)),\displaystyle:=\widehat{\nabla}F((x_{t+1},y_{t+1});\Omega_{t}^{(2)}),

and write g^t(r)=(g^x,t(r),g^y,t(r))\widehat{g}_{t}^{(r)}=(\widehat{g}_{x,t}^{(r)},\widehat{g}_{y,t}^{(r)}). Each batch is drawn independently of all information available before that batch is queried.

Single-loop update.

SPDE maintains the primal–dual iterate (xt,yt)(x_{t},y_{t}), the proximal center ztz_{t}, normal-cone vectors ξt\xi_{t} and ntn_{t}, and a dual momentum vector vtv_{t}. The first stochastic gradient estimate generates the projected predictor (x~t,y~t)(\widetilde{x}_{t},\widetilde{y}_{t}). The second estimate produces the corrected iterate and the associated normal-cone vectors. It also forms the intermediate momentum v¯t\bar{v}_{t} used in the dual correction. After the corrected point has been computed, a third fresh batch updates the dual momentum at that point. This sampling order makes the endpoint gradient error conditionally mean zero given the corrected iterate and its normal-cone vectors. Finally, the relaxed update zt+1=(1−β)​zt+β​xt+1z_{t+1}=(1-\beta)z_{t}+\beta x_{t+1} moves the proximal center toward the corrected primal iterate. Thus the center evolves together with the predictor–corrector and momentum updates, without a separate outer loop.

The coupling of the normal-cone corrections with the damped dual momentum is a central feature of SPDE. In particular, the scaling of nt+1n_{t+1} by 1+k1+k is part of this coupling, and the same vector enters the next momentum update. Algorithm 1 gives the complete procedure. The convergence results below specify admissible parameter choices within the ranges stated in the algorithm.

The output rule is used for the GS guarantees in this section. It requires no evaluation of the stationarity residual. The output used for the OS guarantees is specified in Section 5.

3.1 Stochastic oracle and batch errors

We next state the stochastic oracle assumptions and describe the information available at each query. These assumptions connect sample gradients to the population gradient; differentiability of the sample losses alone does not assert unbiasedness.

Assumption 2.

Let 𝒜\mathcal{A} be the sigma-algebra representing the information available before an oracle query, and let u=(x,y)∈X×Yu=(x,y)\in X\times Y be an 𝒜\mathcal{A}-measurable query point. The oracle draws a fresh sample ω∼𝒟\omega\sim\mathcal{D}, independently of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, and returns a measurable sample gradient ∇f​(u,ω)∈ℝn+p\nabla f(u;\omega)\in\mathbb{R}^{n+p} satisfying

𝔼⁡[∇f​(u,ω)∣𝒜]=∇F​(u),𝔼⁡[∥∇f​(u,ω)−∇F​(u)∥2|𝒜]≤σ2.\mathbb{E}[\nabla f(u;\omega)\mid\mathcal{A}]=\nabla F(u),\qquad\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert\nabla f(u;\omega)-\nabla F(u)\rVert^{2}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{A}\right]\leq\sigma^{2}. (14)

Here σ≥0\sigma\geq 0 is independent of the query point, iteration index, and regularization parameter. Within each batch, the samples are independent draws from 𝒟\mathcal{D} and are independent of the pre-query information. Each evaluation of ∇f​(u,ω)\nabla f(u;\omega) counts as one stochastic first-order oracle (SFO) call.

Conditional independence and unbiasedness imply that the mini-batch estimator satisfies

𝔼⁡[∇^​F​(u,Ω)∣𝒜]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}[\widehat{\nabla}F(u;\Omega)\mid\mathcal{A}] =∇F​(u),\displaystyle=\nabla F(u), (15)
𝔼⁡[∥∇^​F​(u,Ω)−∇F​(u)∥2|𝒜]\displaystyle\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert\widehat{\nabla}F(u;\Omega)-\nabla F(u)\rVert^{2}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{A}\right] ≤σ2m.\displaystyle\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{m}.

Indeed, the cross terms between distinct sample-gradient errors have zero conditional expectation. No smoothness or concavity assumption is imposed on individual sample losses beyond the differentiability in Assumption 1. All smoothness and concavity properties used in this section concern the population objective FF. In particular, SPDE does not require the mean-square Lipschitz condition used later for VR-SPDE.

Oracle accounting.

Every occurrence of g^t(1)\widehat{g}_{t}^{(1)} within iteration tt uses the same computed vector. The third batch is used for the endpoint momentum update, and the first batch of iteration t+1t+1 is drawn afresh. With three batches of size mm per iteration, Algorithm 1, as written, uses 3​m​T3mT SFO calls. Only the yy component of the third estimate enters the updates; if an implementation evaluates only that component, we still charge one full-gradient SFO call per sample. Thus 3​m​T3mT is also a valid upper bound under this convention.

Filtration and conditional errors.

Let ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t} be the sigma-algebra generated by all oracle samples drawn before iteration tt, together with the deterministic initialization. Define

ℱt(1):=σ⁡(ℱt,Ωt(0)),ℱt(2):=σ⁡(ℱt(1),Ωt(1)),ℱt+1:=σ⁡(ℱt(2),Ωt(2)).\mathcal{F}_{t}^{(1)}:=\sigma(\mathcal{F}_{t},\Omega_{t}^{(0)}),\qquad\mathcal{F}_{t}^{(2)}:=\sigma(\mathcal{F}_{t}^{(1)},\Omega_{t}^{(1)}),\qquad\mathcal{F}_{t+1}:=\sigma(\mathcal{F}_{t}^{(2)},\Omega_{t}^{(2)}).

The state (xt,yt,zt,ξt,nt,vt)(x_{t},y_{t},z_{t},\xi_{t},n_{t},v_{t}) is ℱt\mathcal{F}_{t}-measurable. The predictor (x~t,y~t)(\widetilde{x}_{t},\widetilde{y}_{t}) is ℱt(1)\mathcal{F}_{t}^{(1)}-measurable, and the corrected quantities xt+1,yt+1,ξt+1,nt+1x_{t+1},y_{t+1},\xi_{t+1},n_{t+1} and v¯t\bar{v}_{t} are ℱt(2)\mathcal{F}_{t}^{(2)}-measurable. The center zt+1z_{t+1} is also ℱt(2)\mathcal{F}_{t}^{(2)}-measurable, because its update does not depend on the third batch.

Define the batch errors by

at\displaystyle a_{t} :=g^t(0)−∇F​(xt,yt),\displaystyle:=\widehat{g}_{t}^{(0)}-\nabla F(x_{t},y_{t}), (16)
bt\displaystyle b_{t} :=g^t(1)−∇F​(x~t,y~t),\displaystyle:=\widehat{g}_{t}^{(1)}-\nabla F(\widetilde{x}_{t},\widetilde{y}_{t}),
ct\displaystyle c_{t} :=g^t(2)−∇F​(xt+1,yt+1).\displaystyle:=\widehat{g}_{t}^{(2)}-\nabla F(x_{t+1},y_{t+1}).

Equivalently, the stochastic estimates admit the decompositions

g^t(0)\displaystyle\widehat{g}_{t}^{(0)} =∇F​(xt,yt)+at,\displaystyle=\nabla F(x_{t},y_{t})+a_{t}, (17)
g^t(1)\displaystyle\widehat{g}_{t}^{(1)} =∇F​(x~t,y~t)+bt,\displaystyle=\nabla F(\widetilde{x}_{t},\widetilde{y}_{t})+b_{t},
g^t(2)\displaystyle\widehat{g}_{t}^{(2)} =∇F​(xt+1,yt+1)+ct.\displaystyle=\nabla F(x_{t+1},y_{t+1})+c_{t}.

Applying (15) at the three successive query points gives

𝔼[at∣ℱt]=0,𝔼[bt∣ℱt(1)]=0,𝔼[ct∣ℱt(2)]=0,𝔼[∥at∥2∣ℱt]≤σ2m,𝔼[∥bt∥2∣ℱt(1)]≤σ2m,𝔼[∥ct∥2∣ℱt(2)]≤σ2m.\begin{gathered}\mathbb{E}[a_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}[b_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}^{(1)}]=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}[c_{t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}^{(2)}]=0,\\ \mathbb{E}[\lVert a_{t}\rVert^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}]\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{m},\qquad\mathbb{E}[\lVert b_{t}\rVert^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}^{(1)}]\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{m},\qquad\mathbb{E}[\lVert c_{t}\rVert^{2}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}^{(2)}]\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{m}.\end{gathered} (18)

Writing ct=(cx,t,cy,t)c_{t}=(c_{x,t},c_{y,t}), the endpoint momentum update therefore takes the form

vt+1=α​vt+k⁡(∇yF​(xt+1,yt+1)−τ​yt+1−nt+1)+k​cy,t,𝔼⁡[cy,t∣ℱt(2)]=0.v_{t+1}=\alpha v_{t}+k\bigl(\nabla_{y}F(x_{t+1},y_{t+1})-\tau y_{t+1}-n_{t+1}\bigr)+kc_{y,t},\qquad\mathbb{E}[c_{y,t}\mid\mathcal{F}_{t}^{(2)}]=0.

This identity states precisely the conditional centering supplied by the third batch. The errors ata_{t}, btb_{t}, and ctc_{t} need not be mutually independent, since their query points depend on preceding batches; the analysis uses their conditional moment properties in (18).

The deterministic saddle-point, envelope, sensitivity, and normal-cone arguments below concern the population objective. For the stochastic updates, we first substitute (17) into the algorithm and derive inequalities for the realized iterates and errors. We then take conditional expectations with respect to the appropriate sigma-algebras. In particular, conditional mean-zero identities are used only when the other factors are measurable with respect to the corresponding pre-query information.

Lemma 1.

Suppose that Assumptions 1 and 2 hold, and let the iterates be generated by Algorithm 1. Then, almost surely, for every t=0,…,Tt=0,\ldots,T,

xt,zt∈X,yt∈Y,ξt∈NX​(xt),nt∈NY​(yt).x_{t},z_{t}\in X,\qquad y_{t}\in Y,\qquad\xi_{t}\in N_{X}(x_{t}),\qquad n_{t}\in N_{Y}(y_{t}). (19)

The predictors satisfy (x~t,y~t)∈X×Y(\widetilde{x}_{t},\widetilde{y}_{t})\in X\times Y for t=0,…,T−1t=0,\ldots,T-1. At every finite iteration, all state components, predictors, intermediate momentum vectors, and batch gradient estimates have finite second moments.

Proof.

The initialization is feasible, and the zero vector belongs to the normal cone at every point of a nonempty closed convex set. The projection steps ensure that the predictors and corrected iterates are feasible. Since 0<β≤10<\beta\leq 1,

zt+1=(1−β)​zt+β​xt+1∈Xz_{t+1}=(1-\beta)z_{t}+\beta x_{t+1}\in X

whenever zt,xt+1∈Xz_{t},x_{t+1}\in X.

By the projection optimality condition in (5), the primal correction satisfies

xt−h⁡(g^x,t(1)+2​L​(x~t−zt))−xt+1=h​ξt+1∈NX​(xt+1).x_{t}-h\bigl(\widehat{g}_{x,t}^{(1)}+2L(\widetilde{x}_{t}-z_{t})\bigr)-x_{t+1}=h\xi_{t+1}\in N_{X}(x_{t+1}).

Similarly, the dual correction gives

yt+h⁡(g^y,t(1)−τ​y~t+v¯t)−yt+1=h⁡(1+k)​nt+1∈NY​(yt+1).y_{t}+h\bigl(\widehat{g}_{y,t}^{(1)}-\tau\widetilde{y}_{t}+\bar{v}_{t}\bigr)-y_{t+1}=h(1+k)n_{t+1}\in N_{Y}(y_{t+1}).

Normal cones are cones, and h>0h>0 and 1+k>01+k>0. Dividing by these positive scalars proves (19) by induction.

To establish the second-moment claim, fix uref∈X×Yu_{\rm ref}\in X\times Y. The Lipschitz bound (2) implies

∥∇F​(u)∥2≤2​∥∇F​(uref)∥2+2​L2​∥u−uref∥2,u∈X×Y.\lVert\nabla F(u)\rVert^{2}\leq 2\lVert\nabla F(u_{\rm ref})\rVert^{2}+2L^{2}\lVert u-u_{\rm ref}\rVert^{2},\qquad u\in X\times Y.

For any square-integrable feasible query point uu, conditional unbiasedness and (15) yield

𝔼⁡[∥∇^​F​(u,Ω)∥2|𝒜]≤∥∇F​(u)∥2+σ2m.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert\widehat{\nabla}F(u;\Omega)\rVert^{2}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{A}\right]\leq\lVert\nabla F(u)\rVert^{2}+\frac{\sigma^{2}}{m}.

Hence the corresponding batch estimate has a finite second moment.

Moreover, for any nonempty closed convex set CC and any fixed uC∈Cu_{C}\in C, nonexpansiveness gives

∥ΠC​(w)−uC∥=∥ΠC​(w)−ΠC​(uC)∥≤∥w−uC∥.\lVert\Pi_{C}(w)-u_{C}\rVert=\lVert\Pi_{C}(w)-\Pi_{C}(u_{C})\rVert\leq\lVert w-u_{C}\rVert.

Thus projection preserves finite second moments. Starting from the deterministic initialization, apply these observations successively to the first batch and predictor, the second batch and correction, and the third batch and momentum update. All remaining updates are affine combinations with fixed finite coefficients. Induction establishes the claimed finite second moments at every finite iteration. ∎

3.2 Convergence analysis

We now introduce the regularized saddle point attached to a fixed center and the potential that will telescope across iterations. The first three results establish sensitivity, nonnegativity, and an accuracy-independent initial budget; none of them uses stochastic independence.

For a fixed center z∈ℝnz\in\mathbb{R}^{n}, define

p⁡(z):=minx∈X⁡maxy∈Y⁡G⁡(x,y,z),(x⋆​(z),y⋆​(z)):=the unique saddle point of G⁡(⋅,⋅,z).\begin{gathered}p(z):=\min_{x\in X}\max_{y\in Y}G(x,y;z),\\ (x^{\star}(z),y^{\star}(z)):=\text{the unique saddle point of $G(\cdot,\cdot;z)$}.\end{gathered} (20)

Existence follows from strong convexity and coercivity in xx, compactness of YY, and the convex–concave minimax theorem. Strong convexity and strong concavity give uniqueness. More explicitly, for fixed y∈Yy\in Y, the function G⁡(x,y,z)G(x,y;z) has a quadratic lower bound. Thus maxy⁡G⁡(x,y,z)\max_{y}G(x,y;z) has bounded sublevel sets and attains its minimum. The convex–concave minimax theorem can be applied on a compact convex subset containing all relevant minimizers; coercivity then recovers the problem over XX.

Lemma 2.

Suppose that Assumption 1 holds and 0<τ≤L0<\tau\leq L. Then, for all z,z′∈ℝnz,z^{\prime}\in\mathbb{R}^{n},

∥x⋆​(z′)−x⋆​(z)∥≤2​∥z′−z∥,∥y⋆​(z′)−y⋆​(z)∥≤2​Lτ​∥z′−z∥,\lVert x^{\star}(z^{\prime})-x^{\star}(z)\rVert\leq 2\lVert z^{\prime}-z\rVert,\qquad\lVert y^{\star}(z^{\prime})-y^{\star}(z)\rVert\leq\sqrt{\frac{2L}{\tau}}\lVert z^{\prime}-z\rVert, (21)

and

∇p​(z)=2​L​(z−x⋆​(z)),∥∇p​(z′)−∇p​(z)∥≤6​L​∥z′−z∥.\nabla p(z)=2L(z-x^{\star}(z)),\qquad\lVert\nabla p(z^{\prime})-\nabla p(z)\rVert\leq 6L\lVert z^{\prime}-z\rVert. (22)
Proof.

Define 𝒯⁡(x,y)=(∇xF​(x,y)+2​L​x,−∇yF​(x,y)+τ​y)\mathcal{T}(x,y)=(\nabla_{x}F(x,y)+2Lx,-\nabla_{y}F(x,y)+\tau y). Adding the two pairs of first-order strong convexity and strong concavity inequalities for GG gives

⟨𝒯⁡(x′,y′)−𝒯⁡(x,y),(x′−x,y′−y)⟩≥L​∥x′−x∥2+τ​∥y′−y∥2.\langle\mathcal{T}(x^{\prime},y^{\prime})-\mathcal{T}(x,y),(x^{\prime}-x,y^{\prime}-y)\rangle\geq L\lVert x^{\prime}-x\rVert^{2}+\tau\lVert y^{\prime}-y\rVert^{2}.

Add the variational inequalities at the two saddle points and write δx=x⋆​(z′)−x⋆​(z)\delta_{x}=x^{\star}(z^{\prime})-x^{\star}(z) and δy=y⋆​(z′)−y⋆​(z)\delta_{y}=y^{\star}(z^{\prime})-y^{\star}(z). Then

L​∥δx∥2+τ​∥δy∥2≤2​L​⟨z′−z,δx⟩≤L2​∥δx∥2+2​L​∥z′−z∥2.L\lVert\delta_{x}\rVert^{2}+\tau\lVert\delta_{y}\rVert^{2}\leq 2L\langle z^{\prime}-z,\delta_{x}\rangle\leq\frac{L}{2}\lVert\delta_{x}\rVert^{2}+2L\lVert z^{\prime}-z\rVert^{2}.

Rearranging proves (21). Let ϕτ​(x)=maxy∈Y⁡{F⁡(x,y)−τ​∥y∥2/2}\phi_{\tau}(x)=\max_{y\in Y}\{F(x,y)-\tau\lVert y\rVert^{2}/2\}. Then p⁡(z)=minx∈X⁡{ϕτ​(x)+L​∥x−z∥2}p(z)=\min_{x\in X}\{\phi_{\tau}(x)+L\lVert x-z\rVert^{2}\}. Uniqueness of the minimizer and envelope differentiation give ∇p​(z)=2​L​(z−x⋆​(z))\nabla p(z)=2L(z-x^{\star}(z)). Together with (21), this yields the Lipschitz bound 2​L​(1+2)=6​L2L(1+2)=6L. ∎

The potential used in the remaining concave analysis employs the shorthand

s:=2​L​τ.s:=\sqrt{2L\tau}. (23)

Write wt=(xt,yt,ξt,nt,vt)w_{t}=(x_{t},y_{t},\xi_{t},n_{t},v_{t}). For w=(x,y,ξ,n,v)w=(x,y,\xi,n,v) with ξ∈NX​(x),n∈NY​(y)\xi\in N_{X}(x),n\in N_{Y}(y), define

+1L​∥−∇yG​(x,y,z)+n−v∥2+s16​L​⟨v,y−y⋆​(z)⟩+τ256​∥y−y⋆​(z)∥2,\displaystyle+\frac{1}{L}\lVert-\nabla_{y}G(x,y;z)+n-v\rVert^{2}+\frac{s}{16L}\langle v,y-y^{\star}(z)\rangle+\frac{\tau}{256}\lVert y-y^{\star}(z)\rVert^{2},

The next lemma is the deterministic algebraic core of the analysis. It isolates one predictor–corrector step at a fixed center and keeps the two gradient errors explicit. In the SPDE proof these errors are the realized sample-gradient errors generated by Ωt(0)\Omega_{t}^{(0)} and Ωt(1)\Omega_{t}^{(1)}; in the VR-SPDE proof they are the errors of the recursive sample estimator.

Throughout this subsection, the center zz is fixed. All gradients refer to the same function G⁡(⋅,⋅,z)G(\cdot,\cdot;z), so neither conditional expectations nor center updates arise here. The next lemma makes the concrete step-size and damping choices at their first use. Consider two feasible states w=(x,y,ξ,n,v)w=(x,y,\xi,n,v) and w+=(x+,y+,ξ+,n+,v+)w^{+}=(x^{+},y^{+},\xi^{+},n^{+},v^{+}), and assume normal cone membership at both endpoints. Specifically, ξ∈NX​(x)\xi\in N_{X}(x), ξ+∈NX​(x+)\xi^{+}\in N_{X}(x^{+}), n∈NY​(y)n\in N_{Y}(y), and n+∈NY​(y+)n^{+}\in N_{Y}(y^{+}). For compact notation, define

P\displaystyle P =∇xG​(x,y,z)+ξ,\displaystyle=\nabla_{x}G(x,y;z)+\xi, P+\displaystyle P^{+} =∇xG​(x+,y+,z)+ξ+,\displaystyle=\nabla_{x}G(x^{+},y^{+};z)+\xi^{+},
R\displaystyle R =−∇yG​(x,y,z)+n,\displaystyle=-\nabla_{y}G(x,y;z)+n, R+\displaystyle R^{+} =−∇yG​(x+,y+,z)+n+,\displaystyle=-\nabla_{y}G(x^{+},y^{+};z)+n^{+},

Remark 1.

The theorem provides an upper bound for a general unbiased oracle with bounded variance, using a fixed batch size while retaining the single-loop structure. The O⁡(ε−5)O(\varepsilon^{-5}) bound counts individual sample-gradient calls; the iteration count is O(ε−5/2)O(\varepsilon^{-5/2}). The guarantee concerns the expected squared game-stationarity residual of the original problem.

4 A variance-reduced SPDE method

We develop a variance-reduced variant of SPDE, termed VR-SPDE, that preserves its single-loop structure. The method maintains one recursive gradient estimator along the entire sequence of current, predictor, and corrected query points. This estimator replaces the three independent mini-batch estimates in Algorithm 1, while the projected steps, normal-cone corrections, dual momentum recursion, and proximal-center update retain the same formulas. Periodic refreshes update only the gradient estimator and require no inner optimization procedure.

The recursive estimator introduces a distinct analytical difficulty. In the mini-batch analysis, the fresh endpoint estimate has conditionally mean-zero error, which eliminates the corresponding linear noise terms in (88). A recursive estimate generally retains the error from the preceding query, so this cancellation is no longer available. We instead control the endpoint error pathwise and bound the accumulated estimator variance through the motion of the query points. The resulting variance terms are then absorbed into the descent inequality. This approach yields the variance-reduced GS complexity guarantees in this section; the corresponding OS guarantees are established in Section 5.

4.1 Paired oracle and recursive estimator

Variance reduction requires access to stochastic gradient differences evaluated with a common sample. We impose the following additional oracle assumption.

Assumption 4.

In addition to Assumption 2, the oracle permits evaluating ∇f​(u,ω)\nabla f(u;\omega) and ∇f​(u′,ω)\nabla f(u^{\prime};\omega) using the same sample ω\omega. There exists ℓ≥L\ell\geq L such that, for every pre-query sigma-algebra 𝒜\mathcal{A} and every pair of 𝒜\mathcal{A}-measurable feasible points u,u′∈X×Yu,u^{\prime}\in X\times Y, a fresh sample ω∼𝒟\omega\sim\mathcal{D}, independent of 𝒜\mathcal{A}, satisfies

𝔼⁡[∥∇f​(u,ω)−∇f​(u′,ω)∥2|𝒜]≤ℓ2​∥u−u′∥2.\mathbb{E}\!\left[\lVert\nabla f(u;\omega)-\nabla f(u^{\prime};\omega)\rVert^{2}\,\middle|\,\mathcal{A}\right]\leq\ell^{2}\lVert u-u^{\prime}\rVert^{2}. (113)

Samples within each newly drawn batch are independent, and each batch is independent of the information available before it is drawn. Each sample-gradient evaluation at one point counts as one SFO call; evaluating a paired difference therefore costs two SFO calls.

Write χ:=ℓ/L≥1\chi:=\ell/L\geq 1. Assumption 4 controls stochastic gradient differences in mean square. It is stronger than Lipschitz continuity of the population gradient and is used only for VR-SPDE. It does not require every sample loss to have a uniformly Lipschitz gradient or to be concave in the dual variable.

The estimator follows the SPIDER principle [3]. Its use here requires accounting for an adaptive query sequence: each new point may depend on the estimates produced at earlier requests.

A recursive estimator along the query sequence.

Index the estimator requests by j=0,…,3​T−1j=0,\ldots,3T-1 and define

u3​t=(xt,yt),u3​t+1=(x~t,y~t),u3​t+2=(xt+1,yt+1),0≤t<T.u_{3t}=(x_{t},y_{t}),\qquad u_{3t+1}=(\widetilde{x}_{t},\widetilde{y}_{t}),\qquad u_{3t+2}=(x_{t+1},y_{t+1}),\qquad 0\leq t<T. (114)

These points are generated sequentially by the algorithm. For integers q,Br,b≥1q,B_{\rm r},b\geq 1, set

𝗀j={1Br​∑i=1Br∇f​(uj,ωj,i),j≡0(modq),𝗀j−1+1b​∑i=1b[∇f​(uj,ωj,i)−∇f​(uj−1,ωj,i)],j≢0(modq).\mathsf{g}_{j}=\begin{cases}\displaystyle\frac{1}{B_{\rm r}}\sum_{i=1}^{B_{\rm r}}\nabla f(u_{j};\omega_{j,i}),&j\equiv 0\pmod{q},\\[7.0pt] \displaystyle\mathsf{g}_{j-1}+\frac{1}{b}\sum_{i=1}^{b}\bigl[\nabla f(u_{j};\omega_{j,i})-\nabla f(u_{j-1};\omega_{j,i})\bigr],&j\not\equiv 0\pmod{q}.\end{cases} (115)

At each request, the samples appearing in (115) are drawn afresh after the query points have been determined. Within each paired difference, the two gradients use the same sample.

Here BrB_{\rm r} is the refresh batch size, bb is the difference batch size, and qq is the refresh period measured in estimator requests, rather than algorithmic iterations. In particular, the initial estimate 𝗀0\mathsf{g}_{0} is always a refresh estimate. The same recursion serves all three query locations; no separate estimator is maintained for the predictor or endpoint.

For t≥1t\geq 1, the consecutive requests at the boundary between iterations satisfy

u3​t=u3​t−1=(xt,yt).u_{3t}=u_{3t-1}=(x_{t},y_{t}).

If request 3​t3t is not a refresh, every paired difference in (115) is then identically zero. The update can therefore be implemented exactly by setting 𝗀3​t=𝗀3​t−1\mathsf{g}_{3t}=\mathsf{g}_{3t-1} without additional oracle calls. If request 3​t3t is a refresh, the prescribed refresh batch is still drawn.

The VR-SPDE algorithm.

Algorithm 2 inserts the recursive estimator into the SPDE updates. The parameters q,Br,bq,B_{\rm r},b govern estimator refresh and accuracy; the parameters τ,h,α,k,β\tau,h,\alpha,k,\beta retain their roles in Algorithm 1. Their choices for the two problem settings are specified in the complexity results below.

Every occurrence of the second estimate within an iteration uses the same vector 𝗀3​t+1\mathsf{g}_{3t+1}. A refresh replaces only the gradient estimate: it does not restart the primal, dual, normal-cone, momentum, or center states. Thus periodic refreshing preserves the single-loop structure. As in the SPDE analysis, the displayed output rule is used for GS; the OS output is specified in Section 5.

There are

Nr:=1+⌊3​T−1q⌋=⌈3​Tq⌉N_{\rm r}:=1+\left\lfloor\frac{3T-1}{q}\right\rfloor=\left\lceil\frac{3T}{q}\right\rceil

refresh requests. Charging two SFO calls for every sample in every nonrefresh difference gives the total bound

NSFO≤Br​Nr+2​b​(3​T−Nr).N_{\rm SFO}\leq B_{\rm r}N_{\rm r}+2b(3T-N_{\rm r}).

This bound counts all refresh and difference evaluations. Copying the estimate at repeated query points can only reduce the oracle cost.

Conditional estimator errors.

Let ℋj\mathcal{H}_{j} denote the sigma-algebra containing all information available immediately before request jj is processed. The query point uju_{j} is ℋj\mathcal{H}_{j}-measurable. For j≥1j\geq 1, the preceding point uj−1u_{j-1} and estimate 𝗀j−1\mathsf{g}_{j-1} are also ℋj\mathcal{H}_{j}-measurable. Define

ηj:=𝗀j−∇F​(uj),at:=η3​t,bt:=η3​t+1,ct:=η3​t+2.\eta_{j}:=\mathsf{g}_{j}-\nabla F(u_{j}),\qquad a_{t}:=\eta_{3t},\qquad b_{t}:=\eta_{3t+1},\qquad c_{t}:=\eta_{3t+2}. (116)

These errors satisfy the algebraic decompositions in (17). Their conditional moments, however, differ from those of independent mini-batch estimates.

At a refresh request, Assumption 2 gives

𝔼⁡[ηj∣ℋj]=0,𝔼⁡[∥ηj∥2∣ℋj]≤σ2Br.\mathbb{E}[\eta_{j}\mid\mathcal{H}_{j}]=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}[\lVert\eta_{j}\rVert^{2}\mid\mathcal{H}_{j}]\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{B_{\rm r}}.

At a nonrefresh request, write

ηj=ηj−1+δj,\eta_{j}=\eta_{j-1}+\delta_{j},

where

δj:=1b​∑i=1b[∇f​(uj,ωj,i)−∇f​(uj−1,ωj,i)]−[∇F​(uj)−∇F​(uj−1)].\delta_{j}:=\frac{1}{b}\sum_{i=1}^{b}\bigl[\nabla f(u_{j};\omega_{j,i})-\nabla f(u_{j-1};\omega_{j,i})\bigr]-\bigl[\nabla F(u_{j})-\nabla F(u_{j-1})\bigr].

Conditional unbiasedness of the paired differences and Assumption 4 imply

𝔼⁡[δj∣ℋj]=0,𝔼⁡[∥δj∥2∣ℋj]≤ℓ2b​∥uj−uj−1∥2.\mathbb{E}[\delta_{j}\mid\mathcal{H}_{j}]=0,\qquad\mathbb{E}[\lVert\delta_{j}\rVert^{2}\mid\mathcal{H}_{j}]\leq\frac{\ell^{2}}{b}\lVert u_{j}-u_{j-1}\rVert^{2}.

Since ηj−1\eta_{j-1} is ℋj\mathcal{H}_{j}-measurable, it follows that

𝔼⁡[ηj∣ℋj]=ηj−1,𝔼⁡[∥ηj∥2∣ℋj]≤∥ηj−1∥2+ℓ2b​∥uj−uj−1∥2.\mathbb{E}[\eta_{j}\mid\mathcal{H}_{j}]=\eta_{j-1},\qquad\mathbb{E}[\lVert\eta_{j}\rVert^{2}\mid\mathcal{H}_{j}]\leq\lVert\eta_{j-1}\rVert^{2}+\frac{\ell^{2}}{b}\lVert u_{j}-u_{j-1}\rVert^{2}.

Thus the recursive increment is conditionally centered, whereas the full estimator error generally is not. Accordingly, the conditional zero-mean identities in (18) are not assumed for at,bt,cta_{t},b_{t},c_{t} in this section. When a nonrefresh request repeats the preceding point, δj=0\delta_{j}=0 and ηj=ηj−1\eta_{j}=\eta_{j-1} exactly.

Feasibility and moment bounds.

The projection identities in Lemma 1 apply without change, since VR-SPDE modifies only the gradient estimates. In particular, almost surely,

xt,zt∈X,yt∈Y,ξt∈NX​(xt),nt∈NY​(yt),x_{t},z_{t}\in X,\qquad y_{t}\in Y,\qquad\xi_{t}\in N_{X}(x_{t}),\qquad n_{t}\in N_{Y}(y_{t}),

and all predictor points belong to X×YX\times Y.

All states and estimates also have finite second moments at every finite iteration. Indeed, at a refresh request, population smoothness and the bounded-variance oracle assumption give a finite second moment whenever the query point is square-integrable. At a nonrefresh request, the paired-oracle bound gives a finite second moment for the recursive increment whenever the current and preceding query points are square-integrable. The affine updates and nonexpansive projections preserve this property. Induction along the query sequence, starting from the deterministic initialization, therefore establishes the claim.

The analysis below combines a pathwise descent estimate with bounds on query motion and accumulated estimator error. Appropriate choices of the refresh period and batch sizes allow the variance terms to be absorbed into the descent bound, yielding the complexity guarantees for the strongly concave and merely concave settings.

4.2 Convergence analysis

Retain the virtual momentum and state in (71), the quantities ℐt0,𝒟t0\mathcal{I}_{t}^{0},\mathcal{D}_{t}^{0} from Lemma 6, and Pt+,Qt+,Xt+P_{t}^{+},Q_{t}^{+},X_{t}^{+} defined in the proof of Lemma 9. Also write Yt+=yt+1−y⋆​(zt)Y_{t}^{+}=y_{t+1}-y^{\star}(z_{t}). The deterministic error bound (77) and virtual joint descent (80) hold for these correlated errors: their proofs use only the update identities and inequalities that hold pathwise. After inserting (115), the errors at,bt,cta_{t},b_{t},c_{t} are explicit functions of the realized samples {ωj,i}\{\omega_{j,i}\}. The next lemma is therefore proved for a fixed realization of the complete recursive estimator path; expectations enter only in Lemma 13 and the subsequent accumulated bounds.

Lemma 12.

∥u3​t+1−u3​t∥2+∥u3​t+2−u3​t+1∥2≤𝒟t0L​β+∥at∥2+∥bt∥2L2.\lVert u_{3t+1}-u_{3t}\rVert^{2}+\lVert u_{3t+2}-u_{3t+1}\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{\mathcal{D}_{t}^{0}}{L\beta}+\frac{\lVert a_{t}\rVert^{2}+\lVert b_{t}\rVert^{2}}{L^{2}}. (122)

Define the cumulative expected error and dissipation by

ℰT:=∑j=03​T−1𝔼​∥ηj∥2=∑t=0T−1𝔼⁡(∥at∥2+∥bt∥2+∥ct∥2),𝒜T:=∑t=0T−1𝔼​𝒟t0.\mathcal{E}_{T}:=\sum_{j=0}^{3T-1}\mathbb{E}\lVert\eta_{j}\rVert^{2}=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}(\lVert a_{t}\rVert^{2}+\lVert b_{t}\rVert^{2}+\lVert c_{t}\rVert^{2}),\qquad\mathcal{A}_{T}:=\sum_{t=0}^{T-1}\mathbb{E}\mathcal{D}_{t}^{0}. Lemma 13.

Suppose that Assumptions 1, 2, and 4 hold, and let the iterates and estimators be generated by Algorithm 2 with the parameter choices in (33) and (79). Then

ℰT≤3​T​σ2Br+q​χ2​Lb​β​𝒜T+q​χ2b​ℰT.\mathcal{E}_{T}\leq\frac{3T\sigma^{2}}{B_{\rm r}}+\frac{q\chi^{2}L}{b\beta}\mathcal{A}_{T}+\frac{q\chi^{2}}{b}\mathcal{E}_{T}. (125)

(126)

Let r⁡(j):=q​⌊j/q⌋r(j):=q\lfloor j/q\rfloor be the last refresh index. Iterating (126) after that refresh yields

𝔼​∥ηj∥2≤σ2Br+ℓ2b​∑i=r⁡(j)+1j𝔼​∥ui−ui−1∥2.\mathbb{E}\lVert\eta_{j}\rVert^{2}\leq\frac{\sigma^{2}}{B_{\rm r}}+\frac{\ell^{2}}{b}\sum_{i=r(j)+1}^{j}\mathbb{E}\lVert u_{i}-u_{i-1}\rVert^{2}. (127)

ℰT\displaystyle\mathcal{E}_{T} ≤3​T​σ2Br+q​ℓ2b​∑j=13​T−1𝔼​∥uj−uj−1∥2\displaystyle\leq\frac{3T\sigma^{2}}{B_{\rm r}}+\frac{q\ell^{2}}{b}\sum_{j=1}^{3T-1}\mathbb{E}\lVert u_{j}-u_{j-1}\rVert^{2}
≤3​T​σ2Br+q​ℓ2b​[𝒜TL​β+ℰTL2],\displaystyle\leq\frac{3T\sigma^{2}}{B_{\rm r}}+\frac{q\ell^{2}}{b}\left[\frac{\mathcal{A}_{T}}{L\beta}+\frac{\mathcal{E}_{T}}{L^{2}}\right],

where the last line uses (122) and nonnegativity of the endpoint-error squares. Since χ=ℓ/L\chi=\ell/L, this is (125). ∎

4.3 Complexity results

The preceding lemmas reduce the remaining work to selecting the refresh batch, difference batch, and refresh period. We first exploit strong concavity, where no bias term is present, and then impose the same accuracy-dependent dual regularization used in the ordinary concave result.

4.3.1 Nonconvex–strongly concave setting

VR-SPDE applies Algorithm 2 to the query stream generated by SPDE: every explicit dual-regularization term is deleted and the parameters in (100) are used.

Lemma 15.

Suppose that Assumptions 1, 2, 4, and 3 hold and that

Apply the strongly-concave substitution established in the proof of Lemma 10 to Lemmas 11–14. The paired-oracle recursion and query-motion estimate use only mean-square smoothness, projection nonexpansiveness, and the scalar relations displayed after (100); hence their constants are unchanged. The initial potential remains bounded by BB, and the exact original dual certificate again removes the regularization-bias term. Substituting βsc\beta_{\rm sc} into (130) therefore gives (135). ∎

Remark 2.

The iteration order remains O(ε−5/2)O(\varepsilon^{-5/2}) in both stochastic methods. In SPDE, every iteration pays for three batches of order ε−5/2\varepsilon^{-5/2}. In VR-SPDE, a refresh of order ε−3\varepsilon^{-3} is spread over Θ⁡(ε−1)\Theta(\varepsilon^{-1}) requests, and the difference batches have order ε−2\varepsilon^{-2}. The average oracle work per iteration is therefore O⁡(ε−2)O(\varepsilon^{-2}) for fixed positive variance. The stronger oracle in Assumption 4 enables this improvement. The bounds in Theorems 3 and 5 are upper bounds for the same expected squared game-stationarity criterion.

5 Optimization-stationarity guarantees

The preceding sections use game stationarity, which evaluates a feasible primal–dual pair. We now analyze the optimization-stationarity criterion introduced in (10). The same center-based algorithmic constructions, with the OS-specific parameter choices given below, provide this guarantee through the center sequences of SPDE and VR-SPDE without any additional stochastic-gradient evaluation.

For 0≤τ≤L0\leq\tau\leq L, define the regularized value function and its 1/(2​L)1/(2L)-Moreau envelope over XX by

ϕτ​(x):=maxy∈Y⁡{F⁡(x,y)−τ2​∥y∥2},pτ​(z):=minx∈X⁡{ϕτ​(x)+L​∥x−z∥2}.\phi_{\tau}(x):=\max_{y\in Y}\left\{F(x,y)-\frac{\tau}{2}\lVert y\rVert^{2}\right\},\qquad p_{\tau}(z):=\min_{x\in X}\left\{\phi_{\tau}(x)+L\lVert x-z\rVert^{2}\right\}. (143)

Thus ϕ0=ϕ\phi_{0}=\phi, p0p_{0} agrees with the original envelope in (8), pτ=pp_{\tau}=p in the regularized analysis of Section 3, and p0=pscp_{0}=p_{\rm sc} in the strongly-concave specialization. Assumption 1 implies that every ϕτ\phi_{\tau} is LL-weakly convex. Consequently, the minimizer

xτ⋆​(z):=argminx∈X{ϕτ​(x)+L​∥x−z∥2}x_{\tau}^{\star}(z):=\argmin_{x\in X}\left\{\phi_{\tau}(x)+L\lVert x-z\rVert^{2}\right\} (144)

is unique and

∇pτ​(z)=2​L​(z−xτ⋆​(z)).\nabla p_{\tau}(z)=2L(z-x_{\tau}^{\star}(z)). (145)

For the OS results below, the algorithms use the same independent index J∼Unif⁡{0,…,T−1}J\sim\operatorname{Unif}\{0,\ldots,T-1\} as before and additionally report zout:=zJz_{\rm out}:=z_{J}. Storing and reporting this center changes neither the updates nor the SFO count.

∥xτ⋆​(z)−x0⋆​(z)∥2\displaystyle\lVert x_{\tau}^{\star}(z)-x_{0}^{\star}(z)\rVert^{2} ≤τ​DY2L,\displaystyle\leq\frac{\tau D_{Y}^{2}}{L}, (147)

5.1 Nonconvex–strongly concave setting

Strong concavity removes the artificial dual regularization, so the envelope controlled by the descent inequality is already the envelope of the original value function.

Theorem 6.

The NC–C OS and GS parameter choices differ for a structural reason. Game stationarity incurs the direct dual bias O⁡(τ)O(\tau) and therefore permits τ=Θ⁡(ε)\tau=\Theta(\varepsilon). Optimization stationarity transfers a Moreau gradient, whose norm bias is O⁡(τ)O(\sqrt{\tau}), and consequently requires τ=Θ⁡(ε2)\tau=\Theta(\varepsilon^{2}). This reduces the center rate from Θ⁡(ε1/2)\Theta(\varepsilon^{1/2}) to Θ⁡(ε)\Theta(\varepsilon) and yields the O⁡(ε−6)O(\varepsilon^{-6}) SFO order for both stochastic estimators under the present analysis.

6 Conclusions

We developed single-loop stochastic projected damped extragradient methods for smooth nonconvex–(strongly) concave minimax optimization, with complexity guarantees for both game stationarity and optimization stationarity. The proposed SPDE method combines predictor–corrector projections, damped dual momentum, normal-cone corrections, and a relaxed proximal-center update. Its variance-reduced variant, VR-SPDE, maintains a recursive gradient estimator along the same sequence of query points. Both methods update the primal, dual, momentum, normal-cone, and center states within a single loop, without inner iterative solvers for regularized subproblems.

For game stationarity, SPDE returns a feasible pair satisfying 𝔼⁡[ℛ​(xout,yout)2]≤ε2\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{R}(x_{\rm out},y_{\rm out})^{2}]\leq\varepsilon^{2} with total stochastic first-order oracle (SFO) complexities of O⁡(κ​ε−4)O(\kappa\varepsilon^{-4}) and O⁡(ε−5)O(\varepsilon^{-5}) in the nonconvex–strongly concave and nonconvex–concave settings, respectively, where κ=L/μ\kappa=L/\mu. These guarantees require an unbiased stochastic gradient oracle with uniformly bounded variance. With paired sample evaluations and an additional mean-square Lipschitz condition on the stochastic gradients, VR-SPDE improves the corresponding GS complexities to O⁡(κ3/2​ε−3)O(\kappa^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3}) and O(ε−9/2)O(\varepsilon^{-9/2}).

For optimization stationarity, the same algorithms, with criterion-specific parameter choices, return a proximal center zout=zJz_{\rm out}=z_{J} satisfying 𝔼⁡[𝒮OS​(zout)2]≤ε2\mathbb{E}[\mathcal{S}_{\rm OS}(z_{\rm out})^{2}]\leq\varepsilon^{2}, where 𝒮OS\mathcal{S}_{\rm OS} is defined through the Moreau envelope of the constrained primal value function of the original problem. SPDE achieves SFO complexities of O⁡(κ​ε−4)O(\kappa\varepsilon^{-4}) and O⁡(ε−6)O(\varepsilon^{-6}) in the nonconvex–strongly concave and nonconvex–concave settings, respectively, while VR-SPDE achieves O⁡(κ3/2​ε−3)O(\kappa^{3/2}\varepsilon^{-3}) and O⁡(ε−6)O(\varepsilon^{-6}). Thus variance reduction improves the stated OS bound in the strongly concave setting, while both methods attain the same O⁡(ε−6)O(\varepsilon^{-6}) bound in the merely concave setting.

To the best of our knowledge, these results provide the best-known SFO complexity guarantees among single-loop stochastic first-order methods for the respective stationarity criteria and problem classes. The OS guarantees also match the best-known multi-loop dependence on the target accuracy in both settings. Together, these results establish that a single-loop damped extragradient framework can support improved GS guarantees and competitive OS guarantees under their respective oracle assumptions.
